Hi Sahil,

You asked how Ganeshotsav was in our colony this year. Honestly: amazing and exhausting.

Amazing: the aarti on the first night, two hundred people singing, kids in new clothes, Aaji dancing a little when she thought nobody was watching.

Exhausting: the committee boys came to every door with a receipt book and a "minimum amount". Our watchman, who earns less than anyone, paid because they stood there waiting. Papa paid too, then sat quietly with his calculator later. And the DJ played past midnight for ten nights. Mrs Kulkarni's newborn cried every night.

I love this festival. I just don't love how nobody can say "too loud" or "I can't afford it" without being called anti-festival.

Maybe I'll bring it up at the colony meeting. Politely.

Keerthana

qa.a: The watchman, who earns less than anyone, paid.

qa.a: Keerthana feels real joy at the aarti and Aaji's dancing, and quiet worry about forced donations, cost and noise.

qa.a: Politely suggest donations with no fixed minimum and an earlier end to the music, keeping the joy while easing the pressure.

qa.q: What might the festival feel like for Mrs Kulkarni?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni was probably exhausted and anxious, with her newborn crying every night from the late music.

grounding: Shows an observer who loves a neighbourhood festival but sees the pressure of demanded donations, cost and noise on others.

I'm Afreen, and I've watched Durga Puja from my balcony in Kolkata for twenty years, so I think I'm allowed an opinion.

The good part is unbelievable. The pandal in our para this year was built like a glass palace. My friend Aadhya pulled me into the dhunuchi dance on Ashtami, and I don't even know the steps. Everyone just laughs and makes room.

But I also see the other side. The committee is competing with the next para for prizes, so the budget keeps growing. Mr Das, who runs the tea shop, told Aadhya's dad he'd been "reminded" three times to give more. He gave. His face said he couldn't.

And the loudspeakers face the hospital lane.

I'm not against any of it. I'm for joy that doesn't need a receipt book and doesn't keep the hospital awake.

qa.q: Where do the loudspeakers face?
qa.a: The loudspeakers face the hospital lane.

qa.q: How does Afreen feel about Mr Das giving more?
qa.a: Afreen feels uneasy and sad, seeing from his face that he couldn't afford it but felt forced.

qa.q: What change would keep the joy and reduce the pressure?
qa.a: Donations without 'reminders', a budget that doesn't chase prizes, and speakers turned away from the hospital lane.

qa.q: What might Mr Das feel after being 'reminded' three times?
qa.a: Mr Das likely felt pressured and worried, giving even though his face showed he couldn't.

grounding: Shows an observer enjoying a neighbourhood festival while noticing competitive spending, pressured donations and noise.

I live in the flat opposite Nirmala's in our Bengaluru apartment block, so I saw it from my door.

The Diwali committee came round with a printed list: "Fireworks show, sound system, catering. Per flat: fixed amount." Shreya, the committee head, read it out cheerfully.

Nirmala, twenty-one, lives alone and pays her own college fees. She looked at the paper for a long time. "Can I give less? Or help with decorations instead?"

Shreya's smile slipped. "Everyone's paying. It's for the community."

Nirmala went in and came back with the money. She didn't come down for the fireworks.

On Diwali night the courtyard was glorious: lamps on every railing, kids with sparklers, music. I loved it. I also kept looking up at her dark window.

At the next meeting I proposed a "give what you can, or give time" option. Four people raised their hands.

qa.q: What did Nirmala offer instead of the full amount?
qa.a: Nirmala asked to give less or help with decorations instead.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did the narrator have on Diwali night?
qa.a: The narrator felt joy at the lamps and music but also worry and discomfort, looking up at Nirmala's dark window.

qa.q: Why is the narrator's proposal a good one?
qa.a: A 'give what you can, or give time' option keeps the celebration open to everyone without forcing anyone beyond their means.

qa.q: What was the evening like for Nirmala?
qa.a: Nirmala likely felt pressured and left out, paying anyway and then staying away from the fireworks.

grounding: Shows an observer who enjoys a festival while seeing a neighbour pressured into a fixed contribution, and proposing a fairer way.

Monday, Eid night.

Went to Rizwan's for Eid with Sumit from office. I was nervous on the way: do I say Eid Mubarak with a hug? Do I take off my shoes? What if I do something wrong?

We took a box of kaju katli from the old sweet shop. Rizwan's Ammi opened the door, and before I could decide anything, Rizwan hugged us both, three times, the proper way, laughing at how stiff I was.

Sheer khurma, biryani, and his Nani asking whether I was married yet. (No, Nani.) When the family went to the next room to pray, Sumit and I sat quietly in the drawing room with his little nephew, who showed us his new watch.

On the way out, Ammi packed us each a box. Rizwan said, "Diwali, I'm coming to yours. Your mother's chakli."

Happy tired. Glad we went.

Siddharth

qa.a: They took a box of kaju katli from the old sweet shop.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling on the way to Rizwan's house?
qa.a: Siddharth felt nervous and unsure about the customs, worried about doing something wrong.

qa.q: What did Siddharth and Sumit do that showed respect?
qa.a: They brought sweets, followed the family's lead on greetings, and sat quietly with the nephew while the family prayed, without needing to share the beliefs.

qa.a: Rizwan is delighted, hugging them warmly and inviting himself for Diwali, which shows growing trust.

In the small town near Nagpur, Nilesh's family always celebrated Buddha Purnima at the vihara at the end of their lane, and this year Nilesh had asked Tarun to come.

Tarun brought a box of pedhas from the station sweet shop and wore his best white shirt. At the vihara he took off his shoes, sat cross-legged on the mat beside Nilesh's father, and stayed silent through the chanting, watching the lamps float in the brass bowl.

Afterwards, Nilesh's aunt served kheer to everyone in the lane, whatever their faith. The old man from the flour mill clapped Tarun on the back. "You came for our festival? Good boy."

Walking home, Nilesh said, "You didn't have to sit through all that."

"I wanted to see what matters to you," Tarun said. "Now come for Ganpati. Aai's making modaks."

Sami's stomach fluttered. Everyone was watching: his parents, both grandmothers, the neighbours from the third floor.

Tariq shrugged. "Teta says it means you're bigger now in church. You take part properly."

In the catechism hall behind the church in Kottayam, twelve children waited on benches for their first confession. Thomas, nine, kept rehearsing: "I fought with my sister. I lied about homework." His palms were damp.

"Why do we have to tell the priest?" he whispered to Rashmi teacher. "God already knows."

She knelt by the bench. "It's a way of saying it out loud, so you can let it go. After this you're ready for your first communion. It's a new step: you take part more fully."

"What if I forget something?"

"Then you say what you remember. That's enough."

When he came out of the little room, his shoulders had dropped. He sat down and turned to the boy beside him. "It's okay," he said. "It's quick."

In the village near Udupi, the whole house was busy for Ujjwal's upanayana. Nirmala, ten, watched her younger brother sit by the fire with the priest, a new sacred thread across his chest, everyone praising him.

"Why don't I get one?" she asked Amma in the kitchen. "I know more shlokas than he does."

Amma put down the ladle and sat on the step beside her. "You do. In our family the thread has been given only to boys. That's the old custom."

"That's not fair."

"It feels unfair to you, and I understand why." Amma took her hand. "Some families now do it for girls too. We can talk to Ajja about it. And tonight you can lead the shlokas at the lamp. Nobody knows them better."

Nirmala sniffed, still upset. But at the lamp that evening, she chanted loudest.

In Jin's class in Dublin, twenty-three children were making their First Holy Communion in May, and the whole spring was about it: white dresses, suits, rehearsals in the church. Jin, eight, whose family wasn't Catholic, sat in the library with a worksheet during every rehearsal.

"Everyone's getting cake and presents," said her friend Liam, trying to be kind. "You'll just be at home."

Jin cried in the girls' toilets.

Her teacher, Ms Byrne, found her and sat on the bench outside. She listened to all of it. Then she said, "The Communion is a church ceremony for Catholic families. It isn't a reward for being good. It's just not your family's tradition. But feeling left out is real, and I'm sorry."

The next week Ms Byrne asked Jin to tell the class about her family's Lunar New Year. Liam asked the most questions.

Mehak's first period had started on Sunday, and by Wednesday she knew all the new rules: don't enter the puja room, don't touch the pickle jar, sit apart at dinner. Her Nani said it was so she could rest. It felt like being dirty.

At school she hadn't told anyone, not even Arohi. In the biology lab, when the teacher said, "Today, menstruation," two boys sniggered, and Mehak went red to her ears.

Mrs Pinto stopped the class. "This is a normal body process that half of you will have and all of you should understand. Nothing about it is dirty or funny." Then she explained it plainly, with diagrams, and said anyone could come to her with questions.

At lunch Mehak told Arohi. Arohi squeezed her hand. "Mine started in June. Same kind of rules at my house. Let's go and ask Mrs Pinto together."

qa.a: Mehak felt ashamed and set apart; though Nani said it was for rest, it felt like being dirty.

Dear Maria,

You asked why I missed school last week and why there are photos of me in a silk saree on my aunt's status. Okay. It was a puberty ceremony. My first period started, and in our family that means a big function.

Part of it felt amazing: a new saree, jasmine in my hair, all the aunties blessing me, gifts. I felt important, like a grown-up.

Part of it felt awful. The whole family knowing about my body. Sitting in a separate room for days. My cousin asking loudly if I was "impure now".

On the last night Amma sat with me. She said the function was to celebrate me, not shame me, and that she'd keep the separate-room custom short. She gave me a book about what's happening in my body and said I can ask her anything.

I still feel mixed, but less weird. Please don't show anyone this letter.

Chandrika

You want to know what it was like? Okay. I'm Rehana, and I was twelve and at my cousin's wedding in Hyderabad when it started.

My Khala pulled me into a side room and whispered everything like it was a crime: "Don't tell anyone. Don't let your brothers see. Wrap the packet in newspaper." I felt like I'd done something wrong. For a year I hid pads in my maths box.

My friend Pallavi was the one who said, "Why are you hiding them? It's just a period." Her mother is a nurse. She sat us both down at their dining table and explained it all with a diagram on a napkin: what's happening, why it's healthy, what's normal, and when to check with a doctor.

I went home and told Ammi I didn't want to hide it any more. She was quiet, then said, "My mother made me hide it too. You don't have to."

Now they sit in the bathroom cupboard, like a normal thing.

qa.a: Rehana hid pads in the maths box.

qa.a: Rehana felt ashamed, as if something wrong had been done, and kept it hidden for a year.

qa.q: What helped replace secrecy with facts?
qa.a: Pallavi's mother explaining plainly with a diagram what is happening and what is normal, and then Rehana telling Ammi openly.

qa.q: What might Ammi have felt when Rehana said no more hiding?
qa.a: Ammi seemed quietly moved, remembering being made to hide it herself, and relieved to let Rehana stop.

grounding: Shows a girl taught to hide her first period as shameful, and adults replacing that secrecy with health facts and respect.

Hey Sumit,

Sorry I didn't reply all week. Didi's wedding ate me alive.

The good parts first: Didi's face at the jaimala, and Papa dancing to a song from 1994 as if nobody was watching. I cried twice. Don't tell anyone.

Back Monday. You're buying chai.

Akash

You asked about my nikah. I'm Afreen, and honestly I remember it in two layers.

Layer one: relatives. My Phuppo checking the embroidery on my gharara and calling it simple. Two aunties arguing about whether the biryani had enough saffron. Someone asking my mother, loudly, how much the hall cost. My feet hurt, my face hurt from smiling, and at one point I hid in the washroom for ten minutes just to breathe.

Layer two: the moment the qazi sahab asked me, "Qubool hai?" and I looked at Abbu's face. He was crying and trying not to. I said yes three times, and it felt as if the ground under me had shifted.

My friend Trisha told me afterwards, "You looked like you were somewhere else." I was. I was in layer two.

Nobody will remember the saffron. I'll remember that.

qa.a: Afreen hid in the washroom for ten minutes just to breathe.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling during the relatives' comments?
qa.a: Afreen felt pressured and exhausted, feet and face aching from smiling, needing to hide just to breathe.

qa.q: What helped Afreen hold on to the meaning of the day?
qa.a: Focusing on the moment of saying yes and on Abbu's face, the real marker of a new stage, instead of the relatives' assessments.

qa.q: What might the moment have been like for Afreen's Abbu?
qa.a: Abbu was deeply moved, crying and trying not to, as his daughter said yes.

grounding: Shows a young adult at her own wedding feeling pressure and exhaustion from relatives' judgements while holding on to the ceremony's real meaning.

passage:
Hospice care note, Room 4 — family support

Mr Rahman passed away at 5:10 this morning. His grandson Asif, 24, had sat with him through the night.

Asif was calm and very organised afterwards. He called the family, spoke to the masjid about the ghusl and the janaza, signed the forms, and asked me twice whether he had done everything correctly. He did not cry. His hands were steady; his voice was flat.

When his mother, Farida, arrived, she held his face and said, "You don't have to be strong right now, beta. You can do the duties and still cry." He sat down on the chair by the window and wept for a long time. She held him.

What I did next: I gave them the room, brought water, and told Asif that numbness is a common part of grief and that our counsellor can meet him after the burial if he wants.

qa.a: Mr Rahman passed away at 5:10 this morning.

qa.q: What did Asif's steady hands and flat voice suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: Asif was probably numb with grief, holding it back by focusing on the duties and doing them correctly.

qa.q: Which responses helped Asif, and why?
qa.a: Farida telling him he could do the duties and still cry, and the carer giving them privacy and offering the counsellor; both let grief come alongside duty.

qa.q: What might Farida have felt seeing her son so composed?
qa.a: Farida likely felt worried and tender, sensing he was holding his grief in, and wanted to let him release it.

grounding: Shows a young adult handling a grandparent's last rites with numb efficiency, and being given permission to cry as well as do the duties.

passage:
Wednesday night.

Today I lit Aaji's pyre. The priest hesitated when Baba said it would be me, since there are no grandsons. Baba said, "She was Aaji's shadow for twenty-five years. It's her." So it was me.

I kept waiting to feel something. I walked the rounds with the pot, held the torch, repeated the words. My hands knew what to do. My heart felt wrapped in cotton.

Zubin stood at the back the whole time. He isn't Hindu and didn't know any of it, but he didn't leave.

It was only at home, when I opened her steel cupboard and smelled her talcum powder, that I sat on the floor and cried until my ribs hurt. Aai came and sat with me and didn't say anything.

I did the rites right. I'm glad I also got to cry.

Damini

qa.a: The priest hesitated because there are no grandsons and Baba said it would be Damini.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt standing at the back?

grounding: Shows a young adult performing a grandparent's last rites while numb, and finding that being able to cry matters as much as doing the tasks right.

Madhav and Sunaina spread the wedding list across his parents' dining table in Pune, with both mothers watching.

"Saptapadi, yes," Madhav said. "The seven steps are the heart of it. Haldi, yes; everyone loves it."

Sunaina took a breath. "Kanyadaan... Aai, I'd like to change it a little. Not my father giving me away. Both our parents blessing both of us. Is that all right?"

Her mother's lips tightened. Madhav's mother looked at her lap.

"And the gifts list for the groom's side," Madhav added gently. "We'd like to skip that. Nobody should feel they have to pay to be respected."

Silence. Then his father said, "In our time, nobody asked."

"That's why we're asking," Madhav said. "We want your blessing on the changes, not just on the wedding."

Sunaina's mother finally reached over and squeezed her hand. "Then explain the new kanyadaan to Pandit-ji yourself. He'll listen to you."

qa.q: Which rite does Madhav call the heart of it?
qa.a: The seven steps, saptapadi, are the heart of it.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling as she asked to change the kanyadaan?
qa.a: Sunaina felt nervous yet determined, taking a breath before gently asking for both parents to bless them.

qa.q: What made their requests easier for the elders to hear?
qa.a: They kept the rites that carry meaning, asked instead of announcing, explained kindly, and asked for blessing on the changes.

qa.q: How might Madhav's father see the changes?
qa.a: He may feel unsettled, since in his time nobody asked, but he is being included rather than overruled.

grounding: Shows young adults keeping meaningful wedding rites, adapting one and dropping one that hurts, while asking the elders' blessing kindly.

Ma looked up from the cards. "Purohit-moshai has already given it."
"We'll keep the puja and the pinda. Dida would want that." Tushar sat down too. "But what if we also cook for the old-age home she used to visit? She went every month."

I'm Gautam, and when our daughter was born last spring, my wife Vandana and I had to decide which of my family's rites to keep.

We kept the naming ceremony on the twelfth day. Watching Dadi whisper the name into the baby's ear was one of the best moments of my life.

We adapted the forty days of confinement. Vandana rested and nobody expected her to cook, but she wasn't kept in a separate room or told not to touch things.

And we changed one thing completely. In my family, laddoos go to the whole lane when a son is born. For daughters, traditionally, nothing. I told Dadi before it could become a fight: "Dadi, I know you love her. I want the lane to know we're just as happy." She was hurt for a day. Then she ordered double the laddoos and handed them out herself.

Change offered gently went further than I expected.

qa.q: On which day was the naming ceremony held?
qa.a: The naming ceremony was on the twelfth day.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling watching Dadi whisper the name?
qa.a: Gautam felt deep joy; it was one of the best moments of Gautam's life.

qa.q: How did Gautam's way of raising the laddoo change help?
qa.a: Speaking to Dadi early, acknowledging her love, and explaining the wish kindly let her come round rather than feel overruled.

qa.q: How did Dadi react to the change about laddoos?
qa.a: Dadi was hurt for a day, then embraced it, ordering double the laddoos and handing them out herself.

grounding: Shows a young parent keeping a meaningful rite, adapting one, and changing a custom that treats daughters as less, explained kindly to an elder.
